svg.title: Two taxonomies, and why both. The deductive frame has ten labels derived from the brief, applied by weighted pattern rules to 100% of items, each with a published leverage on the goal from 0 to 1: FIT_SIZE, fit and size uncertainty, 1.0; FIT_EVIDENCE, wants proof on a real body, 0.95; SOCIAL_VALIDATION, wants someone else's opinion first, 0.8; TRUST_QUALITY, doubts the quality or authenticity, 0.8; STYLING_OCCASION, unsure how or where to wear it, 0.7; COMPARISON, shortlisting and comparing options, 0.65; PRICE_WAIT, waiting for a price drop, 0.45; BOOKMARKING, saving with no purchase intent, 0.3; LOGISTICS_CX, delivery, returns and support after purchase, 0.2; OTHER, no frame signal, 0. Labels are multi label: 'wrong size delivered, return pickup never came' is both FIT_SIZE and LOGISTICS_CX. Rules instead of the model because a free tier token budget caps model labelling at a few dozen items per run, and the brief needs a denominator covering every item, not 6% of them. Inductive themes come from the model on a stated sample, with shares reported against the items it actually classified, and the run reports the rule and model agreement rate.

div.h2: Ten labels, each with a leverage
div.p: Leverage is how directly a hesitation sits between "saved" and "bought". It is fixed and published per label, from 0 to 1.

span.small: Wants proof on a real body
Unsure how or where to wear it
Saving with no intent to buy

div.p: A free tier token budget caps model labelling at a few dozen items per run. A brief that asks to quantify opportunity needs a denominator covering every item, not 6% of them. Every pattern is printed on /methodology.
"wrong size delivered, return pickup never came"
Forcing one winner is how a fit signal disappears under logistics volume.

Groq proposes themes from the stratified sample. Shares are reported against the items it actually classified, and the run prints the rule and model agreement rate instead of assuming the rules are right.
